subject: Q3 performance cycle -- what's changing and key dates
snippet: Team -- Kicking off the Q3 performance cycle today, and I want to walk through what's different this time before Lattice starts sending you automated reminders that won't explain t
body_text:
Team --

Kicking off the Q3 performance cycle today, and I want to walk through what's different this time before Lattice starts sending you automated reminders that won't explain the why.

The biggest change: we're moving from a single year-end review to two lighter check-ins (Q3 and Q1) plus the annual comp conversation staying at year-end. Last year's engagement survey was pretty blunt that a once-a-year review cycle meant people were getting feedback on things that happened nine months earlier and had already forgotten the context. This isn't meant to double your workload -- the Q3 check-in is intentionally short. Three questions, no forced rating, no calibration meeting attached to it. Its whole job is to surface anything that needs to change before year-end, not to be a formal record.

Key dates:
- Self-reflections open in Lattice: July 20
- Manager check-ins due: August 14
- Skip-levels for anyone flagged 'at risk': by August 21
- No calibration session for Q3 -- that stays a year-end-only exercise

What I need from each of you specifically:
Doug and Priscilla -- your clinical teams are the largest population and the ones most likely to find yet another HR system annoying. I'd rather you tell your managers this is genuinely short than have them find out the hard way and disengage from the next one too. If your directs push back on timing given the Unit 4B situation, tell them to talk to me directly rather than you absorbing that.

Omar -- Lattice SSO has been flaky for a subset of clinical staff logging in from shared workstations. If that's not fixed before July 20 we're going to have a rough launch. Can you confirm status by end of week?

Jenna -- no payroll action needed this cycle, comp conversations stay at year-end as usual. Flagging only so Q3 doesn't show up as a surprise line item anywhere.

Claudia, Tim, Renata, Farida -- you'll each get manager-facing FAQ content from me by the 18th to pre-empt the obvious questions. If something comes up in the meantime that you can't answer, send it my way rather than guessing -- I'd rather field ten questions from you than have inconsistent answers circulating on the floor.

Happy to walk any of you through this individually if it's easier than absorbing it over email. My door's open.

One more thing, since I know someone will ask: this cycle is separate from the annual comp conversation, and separate from the calibration process year-end uses. If your team members ask whether a Q3 check-in affects their raise this year, the honest answer is no, directly -- but the trend it surfaces could absolutely inform what we talk about at year-end, so it's worth taking seriously rather than treating as a formality to click through.

Marcus Bell
Head of People, Vireo Health Systems
(720) 555-0142

subject: Idea -- piloting a nurse referral bonus, want your read
snippet: Doug -- separate from the shift-differential work already in flight, I've been chewing on something smaller and faster to stand up: a referral bonus specifically for RN and LPN rol
body_text:
Doug -- separate from the shift-differential work already in flight, I've been chewing on something smaller and faster to stand up: a referral bonus specifically for RN and LPN roles, paid in two tranches (half at 90 days, half at 6 months) to discourage the refer-and-run pattern we saw with the last incentive program a couple years back.

Rough numbers: $1,500 per RN hire, $750 per LPN hire, capped at $15K/year per employee so we don't create weird incentive concentration. Cost is modest against our current agency spend -- even a handful of referred hires that displace agency shifts pays for the whole program many times over.

Wanted your gut check before I take it further -- does this feel like it'd actually move the needle with your team, or does it risk feeling tone-deaf next to the retention numbers we're already discussing? I don't want to launch something that reads as a consolation prize instead of addressing root cause.

Marcus Bell

body_text:
[DRAFT -- NOT SENT, still deciding whether this needs Elaine's sign-off before it goes wide]

Team,

Effective [DATE TBD], we're updating the attendance and call-out policy for all clinical and non-clinical staff. This has been in the works since the spring engagement survey, where "unpredictable coverage" came up repeatedly as a source of frustration for staff who regularly pick up the slack when a colleague calls out last-minute. I want to walk through what's changing and, more importantly, why.

What's changing:
1. Call-outs for scheduled clinical shifts now require notice at least 4 hours before shift start, except in documented emergencies. This isn't new in spirit but we haven't enforced it consistently, and inconsistent enforcement is its own morale problem.
2. We're introducing a points-based occurrence system, replacing the current manager-discretion model. Every unplanned absence is one point; three or more occurrences within a rolling 90 days triggers a conversation with your manager, not automatic discipline. This is meant to create predictability for managers and for staff, not to be punitive.
3. FMLA-protected absences, approved PTO, and jury duty do not count as occurrences under any circumstance. I want to be extremely clear about this because I know the last thing anyone needs is confusion about whether taking protected leave puts them at risk.
4. Managers will get a monthly report of their team's occurrence trends so this doesn't become something people only hear about when it's already a problem.

Why now: two things converged -- the engagement survey feedback, and Doug and Priscilla both independently raising that the current ad hoc approach means two managers can handle the identical situation completely differently, which isn't fair to staff and isn't defensible if we're ever asked to explain a decision. I'd also rather roll this out now, deliberately and on our own timeline, than have it forced on us reactively after a particularly bad stretch of short-staffed shifts makes the inconsistency impossible to ignore.

How this interacts with existing policy: this replaces Section 4.2 of the handbook in full. It does not change anything about how PTO is requested or approved, and it does not change shift-swap rules, which stay exactly as they are today.

I know policy language like this can read as cold, so I want to say directly: this is not aimed at people managing real, occasional life circumstances. It's aimed at giving managers)
